blocks.text: 二十年来，攻击性网络作战的瓶颈一直是将漏洞转化为可用利用程序所需的专业知识和时间。到了2025年和2026年，这项工作变得廉价而迅速，从数天、数月缩短到数分钟、数小时。打补丁的速度并没有变快，而且对世界上很大一部分系统，尤其是关键系统来说，也快不起来。

blocks.text: 然而，这并不意味着一切加起来就是一场灾难。我们认为电网不会就此陷入黑暗，互联网也不会就此瘫痪。我们确实认为，这会导致类似2003年蠕虫时代和2017年WannaCry那样的疫情式爆发，受冲击最重的是那些无法快速更新的系统，以及少数几个单次入侵就价值数十亿美元的目标。

blocks.text: 利用程序是我们可以跨越23年进行衡量的部分，所以我们的数据从这里开始。但一名熟练攻击者的时间成本在每一步都很重要。侦察网络、让利用程序适配特殊环境、在内网横向移动、拿到报酬：每一步都需要人，而一个人花上几天时间，只有面对能回本的目标才划算。这就是“小到不值得攻击”的含义。小机构从未躲过大规模攻击，但它们躲过了需要人工介入的攻击，因为不值得任何人花时间。

blocks.text: 漏洞利用程序是一种把代码或逻辑中的漏洞转化为访问权限的程序。二十年来，编写这样一个程序成本高昂。RAND 2017 年对 200 多个零日漏洞的研究发现，专业人员编写一个可用的利用程序所需时间中位数为 22 天。漏洞经纪人每个漏洞要支付数千到数百万美元，而相关技能掌握在情报机构和少数资金充裕的犯罪团伙手中。

inlines.text: 打补丁的速度没有变

blocks.text: 2003 年，Qualys 测算过严重漏洞的半衰期，即组织为一半暴露系统打上补丁所需的时间，结果是 30 天。2008 年这个数字仍是 30 天。2026 年 Verizon 数据泄露调查报告显示，完全修复一个已知被利用漏洞的中位时间是 43 天，比上一年的 32 天还长；一年内完全修复的仅占 26%。而就在同一年，漏洞利用成了数据泄露的首要起点。企业之外的情况更慢，甚至永远修不上：2025 年的工业控制系统安全公告中，有四分之一根本没有附带补丁；电网运营商被允许用 35 天评估补丁，再用 35 天部署；FDA 的网络安全规则只覆盖新上市的医疗器械。即便在技术栈顶端，最后一公里也很慢。10 月，Anthropic 报告称，一个未发布的模型写出了一段漏洞利用代码，让无需登录的远程攻击者完全控制使用 multipath TCP 的 Linux 服务器，所利用的内核漏洞已于 10 月 5 日在上游修复。三个多星期后，两大最广泛使用的服务器发行版 Ubuntu 和 Red Hat 仍没有修复包，而 Red Hat 最初将该漏洞评为中等，因为其时间竞争条件很难触发。模型不到一小时就利用成功了。严重性评分仍然假设攻击者是人。买家心里清楚。在我们同事本周发布的一项针对 100 位大型企业安全负责人的调查中，一位金融科技公司的 CISO 说得很直白：“你能更快发现漏洞，但没法更快打补丁。”

inlines.text: 为什么我们不预期会发生灾难

blocks.text: 先从电网说起，因为这是人们最担心的。断电需要的远不止访问权限。电网控制系统使用专用的工业协议，配有旨在限制故障的保护设备，而且往往可以手动运行。有记录以来每一次成功的电网攻击——2015 年和 2016 年的乌克兰——都需要国家团队数月准备和专门打造的工具，而且电力在数小时内就恢复了。美国大型公用事业公司须遵守联邦强制的可靠性与补丁管理标准。

blocks.text: 对国家行为体而言，电网攻击的制约从来不是漏洞利用，而是意图以及是否愿意承担后果。据 CISA 称，中国国家背景的攻击者在美国一些关键基础设施网络内悄悄维持访问权限至少五年。仅有访问权限并不能告诉我们攻击者何时、或是否会制造破坏。

blocks.text: 更难回答的问题是那些不会收手的行动者：黑客活动分子、恐怖组织，以及能让国家撇清关系的幌子组织。他们的约束从来不是意图，而是能力——把访问权限转化为物理效果所需的工程工作。而这正是 AI 所侵蚀的东西。开放权重模型通常比前沿模型落后几个月到一年，而剥离了安全训练的版本已不再是地下做法：Hugging Face 上托管着数千个此类模型，而且据 TechCrunch 报道，自 9 月以来，至少有一家初创公司在出售对某个领先开放权重模型的托管访问，且该模型已去除拒答机制。从业者表示，剥离拒答机制会损失一部分能力，这可能会拖慢这一进程，但不会阻止它。因此我们应当假设，一年之内，一个不受限制的模型就能做到当今能力最强的受限模型所能做的事：找漏洞、根据补丁写出可靠的利用代码、在网络中横向移动并连续运行数周而无需人工介入。

blocks.text: 由此得出两点。机器速度的打补丁，适用于更新成本低、撤销成本也低的地方：厂商替你运行的软件、静默更新的浏览器和手机、位于平台之后且平台能在边缘拦截攻击、同时等待真正修复发布的服务器。它不适用于更新意味着要停止一个物理流程、重新认证一台医疗设备，或者要联系上一个根本不知道设备存在的所有者。而且即便在适用之处，打补丁的速度也有上限。如果修复每隔几分钟就来一次，全部应用本身就成了停摆风险：2024 年 7 月，一次有问题的安全更新让约 850 万台 Windows 机器崩溃，航班停飞数日。超过某个频率，打补丁就会用自己造成的停摆取代攻击。对于图中右下角的一切，目标从修复漏洞转向让它无法被触及，靠隔离、分段和网络层防护，并在失败时提供安全的人工回退。这需要什么，是我们下一篇文章的主题。

已利用漏洞数量。VulnCheck 在 2025 年统计到约 880 个。若 2027 年低于 1,200 个，说明怀疑派对规模的判断是对的；若高于 2,000 个，则意味着成本崩塌已经到来。作为参照，按长期 6% 的比例套用到 2025 年的 CVE 上，约为 2,900 个，相当于每天 8 个。
披露即遭利用。2025 年，29% 的已利用漏洞在 CVE 发布当天或之前就遭到攻击。若 2027 年这一比例超过一半，说明从攻击者一侧看，窗口已经关闭。
修补时间。DBIR 的中位数是 43 天。若 2028 年报告中低于 30 天，说明防御方适应了；若高于 60 天，那整个故事就只剩这个窗口。
野外 AI 发现的漏洞。迄今为止，AI 发现的漏洞中只有 1.3% 被利用。若到 2027 年底仍低于 5%，说明 AI 发现对防御方的帮助大于攻击方。
受害者广度。勒索软件泄露网站受害者数量在 2025 年创下纪录。如果受害者数量继续上升而赎金支付下降，正如我们预期，损害正在向低端市场蔓延。
工业中断。大规模物理中断如今已经发生，却无人认领：10 月，数百家法国超市在一夜之间失去制冷；11 月 1 日，另外四个国家的门店也遭遇同样情况。如果到 2027 年底仍无一起被归因于 AI 驱动的入侵，那么“利用不等于影响”这一判断对工业系统依然成立。
破坏性攻击与勒索攻击。如果到 2027 年，破坏数据或设备（而非索要赎金）的重大事件占比持续上升，说明不受约束的行为者已经登场，赎金数字低估了实际损害。

blocks.text: On the last day of August, a single operator pointed a few hundred AI agents at a print-management server used by schools and offices around the world. The agents built a test lab, wrote exploits for 2 bugs disclosed 4 days earlier, pulled a target list from an internet scanning service, and went to work. From an empty workspace to the first break-in at a real victim took under 4 hours. When the campaign launched the next morning, 11 organizations fell in 26 seconds. By the time GreyNoise finished counting, 395 organizations in 48 countries had been compromised, half of them schools. The model doing the work was a cheap, open-weight one, not a frontier model from a US lab. The agents even ignored a list of 28 countries they were instructed to avoid.

blocks.text: An exploit is a program that turns a vulnerability in the code or logic into access. For two decades, building one was expensive. RAND’s 2017 study of more than 200 zero-days found a median of 22 days for a professional to build a working exploit. Brokers paid thousands to millions of dollars each and the skill sat inside intelligence agencies and a few well-funded criminal groups.

blocks.text: The 2026 field record is short but specific. On September 21, an AI agent chained two zero-days in a help-desk product to break into the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure, escalating “in seconds,” with the agent, in DIVD’s words, “deciding the next step itself.” In May, Google’s threat intelligence group reported the first zero-day it assesses was developed by AI in criminal hands, intended for mass exploitation and disrupted before use. In August, the NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA warned that AI-generated scripts were targeting internet-exposed Siemens controllers in energy, water and chemical plants. The advisory named no new vulnerabilities, only old exposure newly automated. And Dragos documented an intruder using a frontier model as its “primary technical executor” who built a 17,000-line attack framework and reached the boundary between a Mexican water utility’s office network and its control system before being stopped.

blocks.text: None of these is a catastrophe, and the PHP bugs make the point both ways. A week after disclosure, millions of attempts had produced few confirmed compromises: memory-corruption bugs are hard to exploit reliably, and hosting providers and content networks blocked attacks at their edge within a day. But between 2.6 and 4.4 million internet-facing PHP installations remain, with about 80% on versions the project no longer supports and several hundred thousand with no fix at all. Most are old blogs and small business sites nobody would target on purpose. But that is the point: when attacking is nearly free, attackers no longer need to want a target, and a hijacked site becomes a host for phishing, malware or the next campaign. Unlike Y2K, there is no date after which that risk goes away.

blocks.text: The frontier labs’ results explain the field. They come mostly from the AI developers themselves and run without live defenders, so we read them as an explanation for what we see in the field, not as proof on their own. In March 2026, Anthropic reported that several hundred attempts and about $4,000 got its then-current model to two working Firefox exploits. A month later, its next model, which it has kept off general release, produced 181 on the same task. By June it reported going from a released Firefox patch that fixes a bug to a working exploit in under an hour, and from Windows kernel binaries with no source code to 8 complete privilege-escalation chains in 18 hours at about $2,000 each. Independent measurement points the same way: the UK’s AI Security Institute finds the length of cyber tasks frontier models finish unaided doubling every 4.7 months, and in May reported the first models to complete its 32-step corporate-network range and its industrial-control range.

blocks.text: Patching has not moved

inlines.text: Patching has not moved

blocks.text: In 2003, Qualys measured the half-life of a critical vulnerability, the time for organizations to patch half their exposed systems, at 30 days. In 2008 it was still 30. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the median time to fully fix a known-exploited vulnerability at 43 days, up from 32 the year before, with only 26 percent fully fixed within the year, in the same year exploitation became the leading way breaches begin. Below the enterprise, it is slower or never: a quarter of 2025’s industrial-control advisories shipped with no patch at all, grid operators are allowed 35 days to evaluate a patch and 35 more to apply it, and FDA cybersecurity rules cover only new medical devices. Even at the top of the stack the last mile is slow. In October, Anthropic reported that an unreleased model had written an exploit giving a remote attacker with no login full control of Linux servers that use multipath TCP, through a kernel bug fixed upstream on October 5. More than three weeks later Ubuntu and Red Hat, two of the most widely used server distributions, still had no fixed package, and Red Hat had first rated the bug moderate because its timing race was hard to win. The model exploited it in under an hour. Severity scores still assume a human attacker. Buyers know it. In a survey of 100 large-company security chiefs our colleagues published this week, a fintech CISO put it plainly: “you’re able to find vulnerabilities faster, but you’re not able to patch faster.”

blocks.text: Why we don’t expect a catastrophe

inlines.text: Why we don’t expect a catastrophe

blocks.text: Start with the grid, because it is what people fear most. Turning off power takes more than access. Grid control systems use specialized industrial protocols, have protection equipment designed to limit failures, and can often be run by hand. Every successful grid attack on record, Ukraine in 2015 and 2016, took a state team months of preparation and purpose-built tooling, and power was restored within hours. Large US utilities operate under mandatory federal reliability standards for segmentation and patching.

blocks.text: For states, the constraint on a grid attack has never been the exploit, it has been intent and the willingness to accept the consequences. Chinese state operators quietly kept access inside some US critical-infrastructure networks for at least five years, according to CISA. Access alone does not tell us when, or whether, an attacker will cause disruption.

blocks.text: The harder question is the actors who would not hold back: hacktivists, terrorist groups, and fronts that let a state disown the result. Their constraint was never intent, but was capability - the engineering work it takes to turn access into a physical effect. That is exactly what AI erodes. Open-weight models have typically trailed the frontier by months to a year, and versions with their safety training stripped out are no longer an underground practice: Hugging Face hosts thousands of them, and since September, at least one startup has sold hosted access to a leading open-weight model with its refusals removed, as TechCrunch reported. Practitioners say stripping refusals costs some capability, which may slow this but will not stop it. So we should assume that within a year an unrestricted model will do what the most capable restricted models do today: find bugs, write reliable exploits from a patch, move through a network and run for weeks without a human.

inlines.text: We already have examples of what exposed controls allow:

blocks.text: In January 2024 pro-Russian hacktivists overflowed a water tank in Muleshoe, Texas, by changing a pump setting. In April 2025 a pro-Russian group opened a dam valve in Bremanger, Norway, for four hours. In late 2023 an Iran-linked group posing as hacktivists took over water-utility controllers across the US through a default password. Every one hit a small operator with an exposed control screen, and every one ended in local disruption measured in minutes or hours, not an outage. We expect more attacks of this kind, with more capable attackers reaching small operators.

blocks.text: The reason we still don’t expect the bulk grid to fall is not that these groups lack skill. Even attackers with full state capability have produced outages measured in hours, because the grid is built to absorb the loss of any single component. Its protection equipment acts on physics rather than software, and restoration is practiced. That architecture held against states, and it is what holds against everyone else. The risk from unrestrained actors lands, again, on the long tail.

Most of the traffic people depend on runs through a few cloud, content-delivery and hosting platforms that update at machine speed - during the PHP scare they had protective rules in place within a day for the millions of sites behind them. Core routing and naming infrastructure is concentrated, closely monitored and run by organizations with the budgets of what security people call “the security 1%.”

. Within hours, two lending platforms had frozen markets the attacker was using to cash out, and $628 million of leveraged positions had been liquidated. The same day, a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension sat in
Cursor’s extension marketplace

for about eleven hours and reached up to 5,000 developers’ machines. It attempted to plant an SSH backdoor. Cursor pulled it and rebuilt its marketplace. How the package got there remains unexplained.

blocks.text: Two things follow. Machine-speed patching works where an update is cheap to apply and cheap to undo: software the vendor runs for you, browsers and phones that update silently, servers behind a platform that can block an attack at its edge while the real fix ships. It does not work where an update means stopping a physical process, re-certifying a medical device or reaching an owner who doesn’t know the device exists. And patch speed has a ceiling even where it works. If fixes arrive every few minutes, applying them all becomes its own outage risk: in July 2024 one faulty security update crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines and grounded flights for days. Past some cadence, patching replaces attacks with self-inflicted downtime. For everything in the bottom-right of the figure, the goal shifts from fixing the vulnerability to making it unreachable, through isolation, segmentation and network-level protection, with safe manual fallback when that fails. What that takes is the subject of our next piece.

Exploited-vulnerability counts. VulnCheck counted about 880 in 2025. Under 1,200 in 2027 and the skeptics were right about magnitude, above 2,000 and the cost collapse has arrived. For scale, the long-run six percent share applied to 2025’s CVEs would be about 2,900, eight a day.

Exploitation at disclosure. In 2025, 29 percent of exploited vulnerabilities were attacked on or before the day their CVE was published. Above half by 2027 and the window has closed from the attacker’s side.
Time to patch. The DBIR median was 43 days. Under 30 in the 2028 report and defenders adapted, above 60 and the window is the whole story.

AI-found bugs in the wild. So far 1.3 percent of AI-discovered vulnerabilities have been exploited. Still under five percent at the end of 2027 and AI discovery is helping defenders more than attackers.
Victim breadth. Ransomware leak-site victims hit a record in 2025. If they keep rising while payments fall, the damage is spreading downmarket as we expect.

Industrial disruption. Physical disruption at scale has now happened without attribution: in October hundreds of French supermarkets lost refrigeration in one night, and on November 1 stores in four more countries did. If by the end of 2027 none has been attributed to an AI-run intrusion, “exploitation is not impact” holds for industrial systems.

Destructive versus extortion attacks. If the share of major incidents that destroy data or equipment, rather than demand payment, rises through 2027, unrestrained actors have arrived and ransom figures understate the damage.

blocks.text: Twenty-three years of data say patching does not get faster on its own. Microsoft could once make a large part of the internet safer by fixing Windows. This time no single company owns the problem. Our bet is that 2026 looks less like the start of a cyber war, and more like the start of a long, expensive worm era for everyone without a platform to shelter under – and for the few targets valuable enough that the platform itself is worth attacking.
